Adult Thin sharpbelly (Toxabramis swinhonis) attain a maximum recorded total length of 12 cm [Li = 12 cm], a modest size typical of small cyprinids inhabiting freshwater lakes and slow-flowing rivers in eastern Asia. Morphometric studies indicate that the onset of sexual maturity is marked by a total length of 8.4 cm [Lp = 8.4 cm], a measurement that corresponds closely to the size threshold at which gonadal recrudescence first becomes macroscopically visible in preserved specimens. Field surveys conducted across the species range show that individuals of this length are routinely captured alongside gravid females during the late spring spawning season, confirming the functional significance of this size benchmark. The length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of adults yields an asymptotic body mass of 11.5 grams [Wwi = 11.5 grams], a value obtained from the equation 0.00617 times total length raised to the 3.03 power. At the pubertal size of 8.4 cm, the corresponding body mass is approximately 3.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.9 grams], indicating that fish invest considerable somatic growth between maturation and the attainment of their ultimate size.

Reproduction in Thin sharpbelly begins with the release of small, demersal eggs that are adhesive and quickly attach to submerged vegetation following broadcast spawning. The freshly fertilized ovum measures approximately 1.3 mm in diameter, and the wet weight at birth, calculated from this egg dimension, is 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a value that reflects the minimal maternal investment per offspring typical of pelagophilic cyprinids. Egg development proceeds rapidly under the warm conditions typical of the species' shallow-water spawning grounds, with the yolk-sac larva emerging after an incubation period of several days. The chorion is thin and transparent, allowing direct observation of the cleavage stages and subsequent embryonic organogenesis. Following eclosion, the prolarva depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for nourishment, absorbing these nutrients progressively until the mouth opens and the first exogenous feeding begins. This brief endotrophic phase is critical for survival, as the timing of yolk-sac resorption must coincide with adequate densities of suitable planktonic prey in the surrounding water column for successful larval recruitment.

At a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], laboratory-reared individuals of Toxabramis swinhonis exhibit a maximum lifespan of 4 years [am = 4 years], a duration that places this species among the shorter-lived members of the subfamily Cultrinae. Longevity records from wild populations corroborate this estimate, with otolith annulus counts from the oldest captured individuals never exceeding four complete growth rings. This comparatively brief life cycle is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy, wherein early maturation at a modest body size and high reproductive effort are favored over prolonged somatic growth and delayed senescence. The maximum recorded longevity of 1,460 days [am = 1,460 days] at a thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] suggests that metabolic rate and the pace of life are tightly coupled to ambient temperature, as is commonly observed in ectothermic freshwater fishes across temperate latitudes. Field collections rarely yield individuals beyond their fourth summer, indicating that natural mortality rates increase sharply after the third reproductive season.

Spawning activity in Thin sharpbelly is strongly seasonal, with reproductive adults aggregating in shallow littoral zones once water temperatures rise above 15 °C in early spring. Gravid females, characterized by their distended abdomens, carry fully yolked oocytes prior to the spawning event. The weight at puberty, approximately 3.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.9 grams], is reached during the second year of life for most individuals, meaning that the first successful spawning typically occurs when fish are between 12 and 18 months old. Females are batch spawners, releasing multiple clutches over a protracted breeding period that may last several months. The ultimate body mass attained by adults, 11.5 grams [Wwi = 11.5 grams], is generally achieved by the end of the third growing season and represents the upper bound of the species' size range in most lake systems. Sexual dimorphism in body size is minimal, though gravid females temporarily exceed males in total mass due to the added weight of the developing ovarian mass.

Juvenile Thin sharpbelly grow rapidly during their first summer, benefiting from abundant zooplankton and insect larvae in productive shallow habitats. By autumn, young-of-the-year typically attain a total length of around 4 to 5 cm, a growth trajectory that positions them to reach the pubertal threshold of 8.4 cm [Lp = 8.4 cm] total length by the following spring. The wet weight at birth, 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], contrasts sharply with the 11.5 gram [Wwi = 11.5 gram] asymptotic adult mass, representing a nearly ten-thousand-fold increase in body mass over the life span of an individual. Under the same thermal conditions used in the longevity experiments, 20 °C [T = 20 °C], daily growth increments in juvenile otoliths are readily discernible, allowing precise back-calculation of size at age. The combination of a small body size, early maturation, and a maximum longevity of 4 years [am = 4 years] positions this species as a classic example of a fast-lived, high-fecundity freshwater teleost adapted to variable and productive lacustrine environments at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
